title: German foundations
description: Four A1 German lessons: first words, introductions, polite café requests, and numbers for everyday quantities. Native-speaker editorial review remains open.

units.title: Getting around
units.objective: Understand prices and quantities in everyday errands.

units.title: Finding your way

concepts.title: First words and greetings
concepts.explanation: German greetings follow the hour rather than the person: Guten Morgen, Guten Tag, Guten Abend. Hallo ignores the clock and is what you will actually hear most. The habit worth starting on day one is that every German noun takes a capital letter wherever it sits in a sentence, so Kaffee and Nation look like names even in the middle of a line.
concepts.commonError: Say hallo the moment you arrive — Germans notice silence more than accent. Save tschüss (goodbye) for leaving.

concepts.title: Introducing yourself
concepts.explanation: German introduces you with heißen, 'to be called': Ich heiße Anna. The verb changes with the person — ich heiße, du heißt — and keeps its ß. A question simply moves the verb in front of the person: Wie heißt du? Ich bin Anna is the alternative, built on plain 'to be'.
concepts.commonError: Use heiße with ich and heißt with du. Keep the capital letter at the beginning of a sentence.

concepts.title: Polite café requests
concepts.explanation: German requests a drink with Ich möchte, 'I would like'. Once the drink is what is being asked for, the article turns into einen: Ich möchte einen Kaffee, bitte. Kaffee and Tee are masculine nouns and keep their capitals.

examples.meaning: I would like a coffee, please.
I would like a tea, please.

concepts.commonError: Use einen in these requests, not ein. German nouns keep their capitals: Kaffee and Tee.

concepts.title: Numbers and quantities
concepts.explanation: German numbers are worth having as short runs before you calculate with them, and they take a turn at twenty: einundzwanzig is 'one-and-twenty', with the smaller number spoken first and welded to the ten by und. Learn one through ten first, then ask a price with Was kostet?. Expect the article in front of the noun to change with the job it does, and keep the noun's capital wherever it sits.

examples.meaning: How much does a coffee cost?

concepts.commonError: Use ein with one masculine Apfel and zwei with plural Äpfel. German nouns are capitalized.

concepts.title: Asking the way
concepts.explanation: German builds the names of its places out of smaller nouns stuck together, and that is why the article is worth noticing: der Bahnhof is Bahn plus Hof, a 'rail-yard', and it stays a capitalised der wherever it sits. To ask about it, German puts the verb straight after the question word, Wo ist der Bahnhof?, because the question word takes the first slot and the verb must take the second. Directions then arrive as chunks worth learning whole: geradeaus, links, rechts, with dann linking one step to the next.

examples.meaning: Excuse me, where is the toilet?

concepts.commonError: Wo asks where. Wer asks who, and was asks what. Mixing up wo and wer sends you to the wrong question entirely.

concepts.title: Prices and paying
concepts.explanation: German writes a price with a comma where English writes a point, and hangs the Euro sign after the number: 3,50 € is three euros fifty. The price question is verb-second — Was kostet das? puts the question word first and the verb straight behind it. Günstig praises the value; billig also means cheap but it hints at shoddy goods, so the two are not interchangeable in a shop.

examples.meaning: How much does the coffee cost?

concepts.commonError: Nicht goes before the adjective it negates: nicht teuer. Putting it after changes the sentence into something German does not say.

concepts.title: Days and times
concepts.explanation: The German week is named, not numbered: Sonntag and Montag for the sun and the moon, Dienstag and Donnerstag and Freitag for old gods, and Mittwoch, the odd one out, which just marks the middle. Weekdays are masculine, so am Montag. Say morgen and you mean tomorrow; say der Morgen and you mean the morning.
concepts.commonError: Morgen means tomorrow. Der Morgen means the morning. The article is the whole difference, and the capital letter marks the noun.

concepts.title: Family and people
concepts.explanation: German sorts every noun into one of three genders and shows it in the article: der Bruder, die Schwester, die Eltern. Only the masculine nouns reveal the accusative when they are the thing you have — Ich habe einen Bruder but Ich habe eine Schwester. Eltern is plural with no singular at all, and Geschwister does the same job for brothers and sisters together: German keeps one plural word for siblings and no word for a single sibling.
concepts.commonError: Einen Bruder, not ein Bruder: the direct object takes the accusative, and only masculine nouns change.

activities.body: German does not say 'my name is'. It uses heißen, which means 'to be called', so Ich heiße Anna is literally 'I am called Anna'. The verb changes shape with the person: ich heiße, but du heißt, and the ß stays in both. A statement puts the verb second (Ich heiße Anna); to ask, German moves the verb in front of the person behind a question word — Wie heißt du? Ich bin Anna is the other introduction, and there you use plain 'to be'.

activities.prompt: German has a verb that means 'to be called'. Which of these introduces you with that verb?
activities.feedback: Ich heiße Anna is literally 'I am called Anna'. Ich bin Anna also gives a name, but it uses plain 'to be', and Wie heißt du? is the question, not an introduction.

activities.body: Ich möchte is the polite 'I would like'. The small surprise is the article: German says ein Kaffee, but once the coffee is what you are ordering, the article becomes einen — Ich möchte einen Kaffee, bitte. Kaffee and Tee are masculine, and a masculine noun takes einen in the object position. Swap the drink and keep the form: einen Tee, bitte. Both drinks are nouns, so both keep their capital letter.

activities.body: German counts one to ten in two short runs. Ask a price with Was kostet? and mind the noun that follows, because German capitalises it and makes the article agree: ein Kaffee is a label, einen Kaffee is the one you want.

activities.body: German asks where by putting wo first and the verb immediately after it: Wo ist der Bahnhof? The station is a compound noun, Bahn glued to Hof, which is why it wears a capital even halfway through a sentence. Directions come as ready-made chunks, geradeaus, links, rechts, with dann joining the second step to the first. Open with Entschuldigung and the bare question turns polite.

activities.feedback: Wo asks about a place, and it takes the front slot so that ist can take the second. Wer is its counterpart for a person, was for a thing.

activities.body: German writes its prices with a comma where English writes a point and puts the Euro sign afterwards, so 3,50 € reads three euros fifty. The price question is a verb-second question: Was kostet das? places the question word first and the verb right behind it. Günstig means good value, while billig also means cheap but carries a hint of shoddy goods, and the shopkeeper will hear the difference.

activities.prompt: German puts the verb straight after the question word. Which of these lines asks what something costs?
activities.feedback: Was kostet das? is the price question: Was first, then the verb kostet. Wie geht es? asks after someone's health, and Wo ist das? asks where something is.

activities.prompt: Nicht stands in front of the adjective it cancels. Make «Es ist teuer.» say the opposite.

activities.body: Most German weekdays are a small pantheon. Sonntag and Montag carry the sun and the moon; Dienstag, Donnerstag and Freitag keep the names of old gods, and only Mittwoch names nobody at all — it simply marks the middle of the week. The days are masculine, so ‘on Monday’ is am Montag. And mind the capital letter: morgen is tomorrow, but der Morgen is the morning.

activities.prompt: A Berlin calendar marks each day with one word. Which is the word for today?
activities.feedback: Heute is the one. Morgen, Mittwoch and Woche name tomorrow, Wednesday and the week.

activities.prompt: Most German weekdays carry a sun, a moon or a god. Which one names nobody and simply marks the middle of the week?
activities.feedback: Mittwoch is literally mid-week. Donnerstag thunders with Donar and Sonntag belongs to the sun.

activities.prompt: Read the week. Which day does the passage place in the middle?
activities.feedback: The fourth sentence says it outright: Mittwoch ist die Mitte der Woche.

activities.prompt: Build the German sentence for on Monday I work, with the day in first position.
activities.feedback: German likes the day in front: Am Montag, then the verb arbeite, then ich.

activities.prompt: Complete with the noun for the morning, not the word for tomorrow: Der ___ ist kalt.
activities.feedback: Der Morgen, with the capital letter and the article, is the morning; morgen alone means tomorrow.

segments.text: Complete with the noun for the morning, not the word for tomorrow: Der

activities.prompt: Predict the sentence before you write it: today is Sunday.
activities.feedback: Heute ist plus the day. Sonntag is the sun's day, the name sitting in plain sight.

activities.prompt: Give the English meaning: Am Montag arbeite ich.
activities.feedback: German opens with the day and puts the verb straight after it: am Montag, then arbeite.

activities.body: German puts each noun into one of three genders and shows it in the article: der Bruder, die Schwester, die Eltern. The accusative only shows on masculine nouns — Ich habe einen Bruder, but Ich habe eine Schwester. Eltern has no singular, and Geschwister packs brothers and sisters into a single plural with no singular of its own, so German can say siblings in one word and cannot say one sibling in one word.

activities.prompt: All four of these are nouns, so all four wear a capital letter. Which one is the sister?
activities.feedback: Schwester is the sister. Bruder is the brother, and Eltern are the parents, with Familie sitting behind all of them.

activities.prompt: You have exactly one brother, and he is the object of your sentence. Predict the form before you write it: I have a brother.
activities.feedback: Bruder is masculine and is the direct object, so ein becomes einen: Ich habe einen Bruder.

activities.prompt: Bruder is masculine and moves to einen as an object; Schwester does not move. Pick the sentence that says I have a sister.
activities.feedback: Schwester is feminine, so the article stays eine in the accusative. Only masculine nouns change, which is why einen Schwester cannot be right.

activities.prompt: Arrange the words to say this is my family.
activities.feedback: Familie is feminine, so the possessive is meine, and the whole line reads Das ist meine Familie.

activities.prompt: Give the sentence a second sister: Ich habe eine Schwester.
activities.feedback: The plural adds -n to Schwester, and eine becomes zwei: Ich habe zwei Schwestern.

activities.prompt: The word for parents is plural and has no singular. Fill it in: Meine ___ wohnen in Berlin.
activities.feedback: Eltern is plural, which is why the verb is wohnen and not wohnt.

segments.text: The word for parents is plural and has no singular. Fill it in: Meine

activities.prompt: Read the note about a family that has scattered. Which city have the parents stayed in?
activities.feedback: The last sentence leaves the parents in Berlin while the brother and sister are elsewhere.

lessons.title: Prices and paying
lessons.objective: Read a German price tag out loud, ask what something costs, and choose the word for cheap a shopkeeper will not wince at.

legacyExercises.prompt: German puts the verb straight after the question word. Which of these lines asks what something costs?
legacyExercises.explanation: Was kostet das? is the price question: Was first, then the verb kostet. Wie geht es? asks after someone's health, and Wo ist das? asks where something is.

legacyExercises.prompt: Nicht stands in front of the adjective it cancels. Make «Es ist teuer.» say the opposite.
legacyExercises.explanation: Es ist nicht teuer puts nicht immediately before teuer; German will not let the nicht drift to the end of the sentence the way English lets the not.

legacyExercises.prompt: You are at a Berlin café counter with a single Kaffee in mind. Ask what it costs.
legacyExercises.explanation: Kaffee is masculine and is the subject here, so the article stays ein and the question reads Was kostet ein Kaffee?

legacyExercises.prompt: The loaf on the counter is priced at six euros. Arrange the words into a complaint that it is too expensive.
legacyExercises.explanation: Zu is the 'too', and it stands right before teuer, so the whole line becomes Das ist zu teuer.

legacyExercises.prompt: You have finished eating in a German restaurant. Ask for the bill.
legacyExercises.explanation: Rechnung is feminine, so it takes die, and a bare bitte after it turns the statement into a request.

legacyExercises.prompt: The price frame is fixed. Fill its missing first word: ___ kostet der Kaffee?
legacyExercises.explanation: Was kostet is the frame every German price question uses, and kostet agrees with der Kaffee.

lessons.culturalNote: German cafés often expect you to ask for the bill rather than bringing it unasked.

lessons.title: Days and times
lessons.objective: Meet the sun, the moon and the old gods hiding in the German week, and the one weekday that names nobody.

legacyExercises.prompt: A Berlin calendar marks each day with one word. Which is the word for today?
legacyExercises.explanation: Heute is the one. Morgen, Mittwoch and Woche name tomorrow, Wednesday and the week.

legacyExercises.prompt: Most German weekdays carry a sun, a moon or a god. Which one names nobody and simply marks the middle of the week?
legacyExercises.explanation: Mittwoch is literally mid-week. Donnerstag thunders with Donar and Sonntag belongs to the sun.

legacyExercises.prompt: Read the week. Which day does the passage place in the middle?
legacyExercises.explanation: The fourth sentence says it outright: Mittwoch ist die Mitte der Woche.
legacyExercises.passage: Sonntag ist der Tag der Sonne. Am Montag arbeite ich. Am Dienstag lerne ich Deutsch. Mittwoch ist die Mitte der Woche. Am Donnerstag regnet es.
legacyExercises.translation: Sunday is the day of the sun. On Monday I work. On Tuesday I learn German. Wednesday is the middle of the week. On Thursday it rains.

legacyExercises.prompt: Build the German sentence for on Monday I work, with the day in first position.
legacyExercises.explanation: German likes the day in front: Am Montag, then the verb arbeite, then ich.

legacyExercises.prompt: Complete with the noun for the morning, not the word for tomorrow: Der ___ ist kalt.
legacyExercises.explanation: Der Morgen, with the capital letter and the article, is the morning; morgen alone means tomorrow.

legacyExercises.prompt: Predict the sentence before you write it: today is Sunday.
legacyExercises.explanation: Heute ist plus the day. Sonntag is the sun's day, the name sitting in plain sight.

legacyExercises.prompt: Give the English meaning: Am Montag arbeite ich.
legacyExercises.explanation: German opens with the day and puts the verb straight after it: am Montag, then arbeite.

lessons.culturalNote: The week in Germany starts on Monday, so Montag is the first working day.

lessons.title: Family and people
lessons.objective: Give each relative the right article, move the masculine article into the accusative, and meet the plural words German keeps.

legacyExercises.prompt: All four of these are nouns, so all four wear a capital letter. Which one is the sister?
legacyExercises.explanation: Schwester is the sister. Bruder is the brother, and Eltern are the parents, with Familie sitting behind all of them.

legacyExercises.prompt: You have exactly one brother, and he is the object of your sentence. Predict the form before you write it: I have a brother.
legacyExercises.explanation: Bruder is masculine and is the direct object, so ein becomes einen: Ich habe einen Bruder.

legacyExercises.prompt: Bruder is masculine and moves to einen as an object; Schwester does not move. Pick the sentence that says I have a sister.
legacyExercises.explanation: Schwester is feminine, so the article stays eine in the accusative. Only masculine nouns change, which is why einen Schwester cannot be right.

legacyExercises.prompt: Arrange the words to say this is my family.
legacyExercises.explanation: Familie is feminine, so the possessive is meine, and the whole line reads Das ist meine Familie.

legacyExercises.prompt: Give the sentence a second sister: Ich habe eine Schwester.
legacyExercises.explanation: The plural adds -n to Schwester, and eine becomes zwei: Ich habe zwei Schwestern.

legacyExercises.prompt: The word for parents is plural and has no singular. Fill it in: Meine ___ wohnen in Berlin.
legacyExercises.explanation: Eltern is plural, which is why the verb is wohnen and not wohnt.

legacyExercises.prompt: Read the note about a family that has scattered. Which city have the parents stayed in?
legacyExercises.explanation: The last sentence leaves the parents in Berlin while the brother and sister are elsewhere.
legacyExercises.passage: Ich habe eine kleine Familie: einen Bruder und eine Schwester. Mein Bruder wohnt noch in Hamburg, meine Schwester ist nach Wien gezogen. Nur meine Eltern sind in Berlin geblieben.
legacyExercises.translation: I have a small family: one brother and one sister. My brother still lives in Hamburg, my sister has moved to Vienna. Only my parents have stayed in Berlin.

lessons.culturalNote: Familie covers close relatives, and Germans usually name parents and siblings before anyone else.
